title: The Conception of Buddhist Nirvana
shelf_note: Stcherbatsky's study of Madhyamaka nirvana with a translation of Candrakirti on MMK ch. 1 and 25; the scan also carries a Devanagari text of the Prasannapada (p. 481). Core Indian Buddhist philosophy.
structure_note: 676 page records against pages_count 543 and pages_translated 536, so the catalogue fields are stale. The 212 printed_repeats and 18 backsteps fit two separate paginations: the English study in '( 36 )' style and a Devanagari text numbered again from १ (p. 481 = '४४'). The volume looks like a reprint with the Sanskrit appended, which is a structural splice rather than misread numerals. The catalogue title does not mention the Sanskrit text.

book_verdict: The transcription is clean and the Sanskrit commentary is rendered competently. Faults: invented headings, model glosses and markup in the English, a footnote completed past the page edge, and a probable modern Sanskrit edition spliced into the scan.
reader_summary: This is Stcherbatsky's 1927 study of the Madhyamaka absolute, with a Devanagari Prasannapada text bound after it. The transcription is of the right pages and is accurate. The English pane is mostly Stcherbatsky's own words with added glosses and occasional invented headings. Its translation of the Sanskrit is usable but has slips such as 'rabbit's horn' for a donkey's horn.

title: The Creed of Half Japan - Japanese Buddhism
shelf_note: Arthur Lloyd's 1911 history of Japanese Buddhism (Shingon, Jodo, the Catholic mission period). It touches Asvaghosha and Nagarjuna, but its subject is Japan, not the Indian/Buddhist/Jain tradition as a reading room on Indian thought would present it.

book_verdict: The transcriptions are excellent. The 'translation' pane rewrites Lloyd's 1911 English and softens or shifts his judgements. The book sits awkwardly on an Indian/Buddhist/Jain shelf.
reader_summary: Arthur Lloyd's 1911 account of Japanese Buddhism, transcribed accurately from the University of California copy. The English pane is not a translation but a modernised paraphrase that sometimes changes the author's wording and tone, so a scholar should read the transcription. It belongs more naturally with Japanese than with Indian material.

title: Narada Bhakti Sutra (Sacred Books of the Hindus, Vol. 7)
shelf_note: Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. 7 (bhakti sutras and an anthology of Bhagavata verses with commentary). Indian devotional philosophy; it belongs on an Indian shelf, not a Buddhist or Jain one.
structure_note: The title names only the Narada Bhakti Sutra, but every sampled page is from other parts of the volume. Page 8 is the introduction to Sandilya's doctrine, page 114 is the 'SÂNDILYA-SÛTRAM' with Svapnesvara's commentary, and pages 215 and 307 are the 'First String' and 'Seventh String' of a Bhagavata anthology (the Bhakti Ratnavali). The volume is a compound one, and the catalogue identity is incomplete (I7). Separate paginations explain the 116 printed_repeats and 15 backsteps. 370 records against pages_count 335 means the catalogue counts are stale.

book_verdict: The English pages are transcribed well, the Sanskrit verse-and-commentary pages less well. The volume is mis-titled as Narada alone. The English pane parks or drops Sanskrit commentary and on p. 307 inserts a verse that is not on the page.
reader_summary: Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. 7: Narada's and Sandilya's bhakti sutras with Svapnesvara's commentary, and a Bhagavata verse anthology with Sridhara's glosses. The transcription is of the right pages. Its English is reliable, but its Devanagari has verse-number and word misreads. The English pane is trustworthy where it copies the printed English. Where it handles the Sanskrit commentary, it leaves parts untranslated, garbles them, or adds a verse not on the page.
